title: Herpesvirus Edge Cases: HSV Encephalitis PCR, the Lonely VCA IgG and Return to Sport
summary: Choose CSF PCR over viral culture for herpes simplex encephalitis and handle an early negative result, interpret an isolated EBV VCA IgG as uncertain timing rather than past infection, and apply the three-week minimum before contact sport after infectious mononucleosis.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 64 Hit 8 (athletes with IM), Hit 12 (HSV encephalitis, NAAT not culture), Exam Trap 4 (isolated VCA IgG) and Exam Trap 6 (CSF culture vs PCR for HSV). HSV content checked against Bradshaw 2016 (read via a page-fetch tool), Venkatesan 2013 (read via a page-fetch tool) and Simon 2013; EBV serology against De Paschale 2012 (read via a page-fetch tool) and Balfour 2015; return to play against Becker 2014 and Balfour 2015. Hit 12’s “most common cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis” is taught in the source wording (“most commonly identified cause of sporadic encephalitis”); the reviewer’s specific claim that culture is “far less sensitive and too slow” is taught only as “low yield, supplanted by PCR” (no HSV-specific culture sensitivity figure was found in a readable source). Hit 8 is qualified: three weeks is a minimum from illness onset, conditional on no ongoing signs or symptoms, followed by graded return and individualised decisions (register flag rv-im-return-to-play). The EU Concerted Action consensus (Cinque 1996, PMC486570) and Kennedy 2004 (PMC1765650) were not readable (scanned or PDF-only pages blocked) and were not used.

objectives: Choose CSF HSV PCR over viral culture for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis and manage an early negative PCR.
Interpret isolated VCA IgG (VCA IgM and EBNA-1 IgG negative) as uncertain timing and name tests that resolve it.
Apply the three-week minimum and conditions for return to contact sport after infectious mononucleosis.

scenes.title: Two herpesvirus requests
scenes.altText: Invented scenario. Two laboratory requests on the same shift: (1) a 34-year-old with two days of fever, confusion and a right temporal lobe lesion on MRI; the order reads “CSF viral culture for HSV”; (2) a 19-year-old rugby player, 10 days into a sore throat, fatigue and swollen neck nodes, whose EBV serology is VCA IgG positive, VCA IgM negative and EBNA-1 IgG negative, and who wants to play on Saturday. Question token: “Right test? Right reading? Right return date?”

cues.text: Two requests reach the virology bench on the same shift.

A confused, feverish adult with a temporal lobe lesion, and an order for spinal fluid viral culture for herpes simplex. A rugby player ten days into a mono-like illness, with VCA IgG positive and every other EBV antibody negative.
Is culture the right test, is the serology really past infection, and can the player go back to rugby on Saturday?

props.label: Right test? Right reading? Right return date?

scenes.title: Herpes simplex encephalitis is an emergency
scenes.altText: Fact cards (Bradshaw 2016). HSV-1 is the most commonly identified cause of sporadic encephalitis worldwide and causes about 90% of HSV encephalitis; HSV-2 can also cause it, particularly in immunocompromised hosts. Mortality is about 70% untreated and about 5–15% at one year with antivirals and supportive care. Typical CSF: moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis (10–200/mm³), protein 50–100 mg/dL, usually normal glucose. MRI: asymmetric T2 hyperintensity of mesial temporal, orbitofrontal and insular cortex. Treatment card: intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours started promptly; diagnostic work-up must not delay it.

cues.text: Herpes simplex virus type one is the most commonly identified cause of sporadic encephalitis worldwide, and causes about nine in ten cases of herpes encephalitis. Type two can also cause it, particularly in immunocompromised people.
Untreated, about seven in ten patients die. With antiviral treatment and supportive care, one-year mortality falls to roughly five to fifteen percent.

Spinal fluid usually shows a moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly raised protein and normal glucose. MRI typically shows asymmetric changes in the mesial temporal lobe, orbitofrontal cortex and insula.
So intravenous aciclovir is started promptly, at ten milligrams per kilogram every eight hours, and testing must never delay it.

scenes.title: PCR replaced culture
scenes.altText: Method comparison (Bradshaw 2016; Simon 2013; Venkatesan 2013). CSF HSV PCR: sensitivity about 96% and specificity about 99% (Bradshaw 2016; Simon 2013 reports 94% and 98%); PCR has supplanted viral culture as the test of choice. Viral culture of CSF has low yield (Simon 2013). Early-negative card: PCR can be falsely negative early in illness and in children; if suspicion stays high (for example temporal lobe changes on imaging), continue aciclovir and repeat lumbar puncture with HSV PCR within 3–7 days. Pitfall: immunocompromised patients may lack pleocytosis.

cues.text: For herpes encephalitis, spinal fluid PCR has replaced viral culture as the test of choice. Published reviews give sensitivity of about ninety-four to ninety-six percent and specificity of about ninety-eight to ninety-nine percent.
Viral culture of spinal fluid, by contrast, has low yield, so a culture order for suspected herpes encephalitis should be redirected to PCR.

PCR can still be falsely negative early in the illness, especially in children. If suspicion stays high, for example because imaging shows temporal lobe changes, aciclovir continues and the lumbar puncture is repeated within three to seven days.
And a normal cell count does not exclude it: immunocompromised patients may have no pleocytosis at all.

scenes.title: The lonely VCA IgG and the spleen
scenes.altText: Staging cards (Balfour 2015; De Paschale 2012). Usual staging: acute 0–3 weeks VCA IgM+, VCA IgG − or +, EBNA-1 IgG −; past infection >6 months VCA IgM −, VCA IgG +, EBNA-1 IgG +. Isolated VCA IgG can mean past infection with EBNA-1 IgG lost or never made (about 5% never produce it; loss is commoner in immunocompromised people) or a current or recent infection whose VCA IgM is absent, delayed or already gone (VCA IgM is present in about 75% during acute illness). Resolve with VCA IgG avidity (low in the first 12 weeks; low in about half of isolated-VCA IgG cases), immunoblot or EBV DNA. Spleen card (Becker 2014; Balfour 2015): splenic rupture is rare (<0.5–1%) but most occur in the first 21 days and are exceedingly rare after 28 days; examination detects splenomegaly poorly; most recommendations: rest 3 weeks, then graded light activity; contact sport after 3 weeks only without ongoing signs or symptoms, individualised.

cues.text: Now the rugby player. VCA IgG positive with VCA IgM and EBNA-1 IgG both negative does not fit the textbook past-infection pattern.

It can be an old infection in someone who lost, or never made, EBNA-1 antibodies. Or it can be a current infection whose VCA IgM is missing, delayed or already gone. Low VCA IgG avidity, an immunoblot or EBV DNA can settle it.
Whatever the serology, mononucleosis can enlarge the spleen. Rupture is rare, but most happen in the first three weeks of illness, and examination misses many enlarged spleens.

Most recommendations are rest for three weeks, then a graded return. Contact sport only after at least three weeks and with no ongoing signs of acute infection, decided case by case. Not this Saturday.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Send CSF viral culture for suspected HSV encephalitis” (✓ CSF HSV PCR is the test of choice; culture has low yield); “VCA IgG alone = past infection” (✓ uncertain timing: past with lost EBNA-1 IgG or recent with missing IgM; check avidity, immunoblot or EBV DNA); “No palpable spleen on day 10, so cleared for contact sport” (✓ examination misses splenomegaly; rest at least 3 weeks, then graded return).

cues.text: Trap one: send spinal fluid viral culture for suspected herpes encephalitis. No: PCR is the test of choice; culture has low yield.
Trap two: VCA IgG alone means past infection. No: the timing is uncertain until avidity or other tests settle it.
Trap three: no palpable spleen on day ten, so cleared for contact sport. No: examination misses enlarged spleens; wait at least three weeks.

scenes.title: Brain, birthday, bench
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “BRAIN gets PCR, not a Petri dish. A lonely VCA IgG has no BIRTHDAY until avidity tells its age. The SPLEEN sits on the BENCH for three weeks.” Tokens: brain = PCR · lonely IgG = ask avidity · spleen = 3-week bench. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the brain gets PCR, not a Petri dish. A lonely VCA IgG has no birthday until avidity tells its age. And the spleen sits on the bench for three weeks.

Where it breaks: an early PCR can be negative and may need repeating; avidity is only one of several tests and can still leave the timing unclear; and three weeks is a minimum, not a guarantee, because evidence-based return-to-play protocols are lacking and decisions are individualised.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “HSV encephalitis: CSF PCR, not culture · repeat in 3–7 days if early negative and suspicion high · aciclovir first”, “Isolated VCA IgG = uncertain timing · mononucleosis: no contact sport for at least 3 weeks”.

cues.text: Diagnose herpes simplex encephalitis with cerebrospinal fluid PCR rather than viral culture and repeat it when an early result is negative but suspicion remains, treat an isolated VCA IgG as unresolved timing that needs avidity or other testing, and keep athletes with mononucleosis out of contact sport for at least three weeks.

props.label: HSV encephalitis: CSF PCR, not culture · repeat if early negative
Lonely VCA IgG = uncertain timing · IM: no contact sport ≥ 3 weeks

explanation.what: Plain language: cold-sore virus (HSV) can rarely infect the brain, which is an emergency; the lab finds the virus’s genes in spinal fluid by PCR rather than trying to grow it. Glandular fever virus (EBV) is staged with antibody tests; one antibody pattern looks like an old infection but might be a new one. During glandular fever the spleen can swell and burst with a hit, so athletes wait before contact sport. Scientific terms: herpes simplex encephalitis (HSVE), CSF HSV PCR, viral culture, aciclovir, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), viral capsid antigen (VCA) IgM and IgG, EBNA-1 IgG, IgG avidity, immunoblot, infectious mononucleosis (IM), splenomegaly, splenic rupture, return to play.
explanation.why: PCR detects HSV DNA with high sensitivity and specificity, while viral culture of CSF has low yield; very early PCR can be falsely negative, so aciclovir is continued and the test repeated when suspicion persists. Isolated VCA IgG is ambiguous because about 5% of people never make EBNA-1 IgG, EBNA-1 IgG can be lost, and VCA IgM is not detected in every acute infection. Lymphocytic infiltration enlarges the spleen beyond the rib cage’s protection, and most ruptures happen in the first 21 days.
explanation.measure: HSV PCR sensitivity about 94–96%, specificity about 98–99%; repeat LP within 3–7 days if early PCR is negative and suspicion remains; aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. EBV staging: acute 0–3 weeks VCA IgM+, EBNA-1 −; past >6 months VCA IgM −, VCA IgG +, EBNA-1 +; VCA IgG avidity low in the first 12 weeks. IM: splenic rupture <0.5–1%; most ruptures within 21 days, exceedingly rare after 28 days; rest about 3 weeks then graded activity; contact sport after 3 weeks only without ongoing signs or symptoms.
explanation.differs: CSF PCR vs CSF viral culture; true negative PCR vs early false-negative PCR; isolated VCA IgG (uncertain timing) vs VCA IgG + EBNA-1 IgG with VCA IgM negative (past infection); light activity vs contact or collision sport during recovery.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the test of choice for HSV encephalitis, what to do after an early negative PCR, how to read an isolated VCA IgG, and when an athlete with IM can return to contact sport.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old with fever, confusion and a temporal lobe lesion on MRI has suspected herpes simplex encephalitis. Which laboratory test should be performed on the CSF?

options.rationale: Correct. CSF HSV PCR has high sensitivity and specificity and has supplanted culture as the test of choice.
Incorrect. Viral culture of CSF has low yield and has been replaced by PCR.
Incorrect. Bacterial culture of CSF is useful mainly to rule out bacterial meningitis; it does not diagnose HSV, for which CSF HSV PCR is the test of choice.

options.text: No CSF test; wait for the patient to improve on aciclovir
options.rationale: Incorrect. Aciclovir should start promptly, but CSF HSV PCR is still needed for diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old has 10 days of pharyngitis and fatigue. EBV serology: VCA IgG positive, VCA IgM negative, EBNA-1 IgG negative. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Timing is uncertain; VCA IgG avidity, immunoblot or EBV DNA can help distinguish recent from past infection
options.rationale: Correct. Isolated VCA IgG can be past infection with lost or absent EBNA-1 IgG, or a recent infection with missing VCA IgM.

options.text: Definite past infection; EBV is excluded as the cause of the illness
options.rationale: Incorrect. Past infection is VCA IgG plus EBNA-1 IgG; without EBNA-1 IgG the timing is unresolved.

options.text: EBV-naive; the person has never been infected
options.rationale: Incorrect. A naive person is negative for all three antibodies.

options.text: Confirmed acute primary infection, because EBNA-1 IgG is negative
options.rationale: Incorrect. Absent EBNA-1 IgG alone does not confirm acute infection: about 5% of people never make EBNA-1 IgG and it can be lost, so this pattern can also be past infection.

questions.stem: A rugby player with infectious mononucleosis feels better on day 10, and no spleen is palpable. Which advice best fits published recommendations?

options.text: Avoid contact sport until at least 3 weeks from onset, then return gradually if there are no ongoing signs or symptoms
options.rationale: Correct. Most splenic ruptures occur in the first 21 days, and most recommendations advise about 3 weeks of rest followed by graded, individualised return.

options.text: Return to full contact now, because the spleen is not palpable
options.rationale: Incorrect. Physical examination detects splenomegaly poorly.

options.text: Return when the heterophile test becomes negative
options.rationale: Incorrect. Heterophile antibodies can persist for a year or more, and no single laboratory test gives a definitive return-to-play answer.

options.text: Avoid all physical activity for 6 months
options.rationale: Incorrect. Early light activity has not been shown to be harmful; the main concern is contact and high intra-abdominal-pressure activity.

claims.text: HSV-1 as the most commonly identified cause of sporadic encephalitis; mortality; CSF and MRI pattern; prompt aciclovir.
CSF HSV PCR performance and test of choice; CSF viral culture low yield; early false negatives and repeat LP within 3–7 days; immunocompromised may lack pleocytosis.
Isolated VCA IgG has uncertain timing; causes and resolving tests; EBV staging pattern.
Splenic rupture risk and timing; examination limits; three-week minimum and graded, individualised return to contact sport.
HSV-specific CSF culture sensitivity and turnaround (“far less sensitive and too slow”); “fatal” in “most common cause of sporadic fatal encephalitis”.
claims.note: Not taught as stated; no readable open source giving HSV-specific culture sensitivity was found. The lesson uses the source wording instead.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 64 Hit 8 gives a flat “avoid contact sports ≥3 weeks”. Becker 2014 and Balfour 2015 frame three weeks as a minimum from illness onset, conditional on no ongoing signs or symptoms, followed by graded return; evidence-based protocols are lacking and decisions should be individualised (register flag rv-im-return-to-play).
